title: Treaties
objective: After this level you can explain how countries make treaties.
summary: A treaty is a written agreement between states. Signing comes first; ratification binds. Then pacta sunt servanda: agreements must be kept.

cards.headline: A copy of the oldest known peace treaty hangs at the UN.
cards.body: Around 1269 BC, the Hittite king Hattusili III and Egypt's Ramesses II put peace in writing. They pledged lasting peace, nonaggression, extradition and mutual help. A replica now hangs near the entrance of the Security Council Chamber at UN Headquarters. Countries still make their biggest promises the same way: in writing.

cards.headline: Whatever you call it
cards.body: Pact, convention, protocol, agreement: the label doesn't matter. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969) defines a treaty as a written agreement between states, governed by international law, whatever its particular name. Working out the words is diplomats' work: negotiating with the host government was one of Level 82's embassy jobs. Think of a treaty as a contract, with countries as the signatures.

cards.headline: Sign first, bind later
cards.body: Signing is often not the last step. When a treaty needs ratification, a signature doesn't bind the state yet; ratification is the act by which a state consents to be bound. In between, a signer must not do anything that would defeat the treaty's purpose, unless it makes clear it won't join. The pen says "we mean to"; ratification says "we will".

mascot.line: Signing and ratifying are easy to mix up. When a treaty needs both, only ratification binds.

cards.fact: Pacta sunt servanda: agreements must be kept.
cards.context: That Latin phrase is arguably the oldest principle of international law. The 1969 Vienna Convention puts it in Article 26: every treaty in force binds its parties and must be performed in good faith. Article 27 closes the obvious loophole: a country can't point to its own laws as an excuse for failing to keep a treaty.

cards.headline: Treaties: signed and sealed
learned: The Kadesh treaty is the oldest known peace treaty
A treaty: a written agreement between states

questions.prompt: A replica of which agreement hangs near the UN Security Council Chamber?

options.label: The oldest known peace treaty, from Kadesh
The first draft of the UN Charter
options.rationale: The replica is more than 3,000 years older than the UN.

options.label: The Montevideo Convention on statehood
options.rationale: That's from 1933; the replica is ancient.

options.label: The Vienna Convention on treaties
options.rationale: That dates from 1969, not the Bronze Age.

questions.explanation: The replica is of the Kadesh treaty between Hattusili III and Ramesses II, the oldest known peace treaty.

questions.prompt: Why can't a country excuse breaking a treaty by pointing to its own laws?

options.label: Because treaties always override national constitutions
options.rationale: The rule is narrower: internal law is no excuse for non-performance.

options.label: Because only the UN can change a country's laws
options.rationale: The UN has no such power; the rule comes from the Vienna Convention.

options.label: Because treaties in force must be kept in good faith
Because countries lose sovereignty when they sign
options.rationale: Signing is itself an act of a sovereign state.

questions.explanation: Pacta sunt servanda (Article 26) makes treaties binding in good faith, and Article 27 says internal law can't justify failing to perform one.

questions.prompt: Level 32's Constitution was signed in 1787 but took effect only after nine states ratified it. What does ratifying a treaty do?

options.label: It starts the negotiation between diplomats
options.rationale: Negotiation comes first; ratification follows signing.

options.label: It's how a state consents to be bound
It frees the state to ignore the treaty's purpose
options.rationale: Even a signer must not defeat its purpose.

options.label: It hands the treaty to the UN to enforce
options.rationale: Ratification is the state's own act.

questions.explanation: As with Level 32's Constitution, signing isn't the last step: ratification is the act by which a state consents to be bound.
